title: Consistent tilemaps and assets
author: GerardoPellens
selftext:
So I'm looking for tools or instructies to get consistent graphics for a game.

* Lots of pixel art generators out there - which is not my style
* Lots of motion / animation tools - which I do not need at this point
* Tried some tools, but most of them do not do what I need or I can't find the right tools...

I like to work with Gemini's Nano Banano, but fail to get good, consistent results...

* No transparent backgrounds
* No pixelperfect tile dimensions
* Flat 2D vector art is no consistent

I could use some hands on help on how to get consistent results. I need lot's of tiles, characters, .... How do you guys tackle this issue?

replies.author: odragora
replies.body:
The most reliable solution is probably Codex / Claude with a Blender MCP connection. Your AI model creates assets through trial and error, and you then render them with a top-down angle to convert into 2D images and import into the game.

Alternatively you can try open-source image generation models with Controlnet support, probably in something like KritaAI plugin where you can mask areas of an image and re-generate only those when needed. Choice of models depends on your GPU a lot, Krea 2 is one of the best options right now if you can run it, SDXL-based models are an option for a budget GPU. You can find a lot of style LoRAs for any popular model to enforce a specific style.

comments.author: AutomaticArt1401
comments.body:
Nobody's mentioned the option that kills all three of your bullets at once: stop asking the image model for the tile, and have the LLM write a small program that draws it.

Concretely — a Python script with a palette dict and each tile as a grid of characters, rendered out to PNG. Your three problems stop existing rather than getting better:

- transparent background: the program writes RGBA and leaves alpha at 0 where nothing is drawn. There's no matting step to fail.
- pixel-perfect dimensions: the canvas *is* 16x16. Nothing is ever resampled.
- props on tiles: a prop is a separate call writing a separate file. "Don't put the prop on the tile" stops being a request that can be ignored.

Style consistency comes free too, since every asset indexes the same palette dict — the fifth variant can't appear.

The catch: it only works for flat, low-res, limited-palette art. It is useless for painterly work. And you still have to render it and actually look, because the model is genuinely bad at judging its own sprite — I've had a door read as a face and a signpost read as a table.

Stake: I make and sell pixel packs this way, so I'm not neutral.
